reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A locally aggressive but non-metastasising myofibroblastic neoplasm with infiltrative margins and a tendency to recur locally
Occurs in abdominal, extra-abdominal and intra-abdominal (mesenteric) locations, the last strongly linked to familial adenomatous polyposis
Sporadic tumours usually carry somatic CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations, whereas FAP-associated tumours have germline APC mutations
Both mechanisms converge on activation of the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, with nuclear beta-catenin seen on immunohistochemistry
Presents as a firm, deep, poorly circumscribed mass that may infiltrate muscle and adjacent structures
Any young patient with an intra-abdominal or mesenteric desmoid should prompt evaluation for familial adenomatous polyposis
Because a proportion stabilise or regress, active surveillance is now first-line for many tumours, reserving systemic therapy, radiotherapy or surgery for progression
reference.pathophysiology: Desmoid-type fibromatosis is a clonal myofibroblastic neoplasm defined by constitutive activation of the Wnt/beta-catenin signalling pathway. In sporadic tumours this arises from somatic activating mutations in CTNNB1, while in the setting of familial adenomatous polyposis it results from germline APC mutations that stabilise beta-catenin. Accumulated beta-catenin translocates to the nucleus and drives proliferation of spindled myofibroblasts that infiltrate surrounding tissues along fascial planes. The tumour is locally destructive and prone to recurrence but lacks metastatic potential, and its clinical course is notably unpredictable, ranging from progression to spontaneous stabilisation or regression.
additionalDifferentials: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour in intra-abdominal lesions
additionalInvestigations: MRI to characterise the infiltrative margins and monitor for growth on surveillance
Core biopsy with histological confirmation of bland spindled myofibroblasts
Nuclear beta-catenin immunohistochemistry as a supportive diagnostic marker
CTNNB1 mutation analysis to support the diagnosis and inform prognosis
Colonoscopy and APC evaluation when familial adenomatous polyposis is suspected
redFlags: Intra-abdominal or mesenteric tumour indicating possible familial adenomatous polyposis
Progressive growth causing compression of bowel, vessels or nerves
Rapid enlargement in a critical anatomical site threatening function
Recurrence after resection with worsening infiltration
reference.prognosis: Desmoid-type fibromatosis does not metastasise but is locally aggressive with a significant local recurrence rate. The course is highly variable, and a meaningful proportion stabilise or regress, which underpins the shift towards active surveillance rather than immediate intervention.
pitfalls: Proceeding to aggressive surgery when active surveillance may suffice, given unpredictable behaviour
Missing an underlying familial adenomatous polyposis in a young patient with a mesenteric tumour
Mistaking an infiltrative desmoid for a sarcoma or vice versa without beta-catenin and molecular testing
Assuming clear margins guarantee cure, given the notable recurrence rate
